extracted.intended_audience: students, teachers, and practitioners interested in the philosophy and method of science (educated lay readers and scientifically-minded citizens)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts criteria and standards for good science, scientific language, inference, law, causation, and classification of the sciences as presented in Karl Pearson's The Grammar of Science. Aimed at guiding how to form scientific judgments and how to teach/evaluate scientific work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of facts and impartial judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: The classification of facts and the formation of absolute judgments upon the basis of this classification — judgments independent of the idiosyncrasies of the individual mind — is peculiarly the scope and method of modern science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Science must base judgments on clear knowledge of facts, appreciate their sequence and relative significance, and form judgments that are independent of the individual mind (i.e., remove personal bias). The classification of facts and recognition of their sequence is central to producing judgments useful for citizenship and policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim at self-elimination in scientific judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: The scientific man has above all things to aim at self-elimination in his judgments, to provide an argument which is as true for each individual mind as for his own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientific practice requires methods and presentation that minimise the influence of the particular observer's feelings or prejudices; arguments should be constructed so others can reach the same conclusion from the same facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habit of dispassionate investigation (the scientific frame of mind)
rubrics_metrics.description: The habit of forming a judgment upon classified facts unbiased by personal feeling is characteristic of the scientific frame of mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate dispassionate, objective assessment of evidence; this mental habit is a criterion for good scientific practice and an essential quality for citizens making public judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appreciation of method over memorized facts in education
rubrics_metrics.description: The true aim of the teacher must be to impart an appreciation of method and not a knowledge of facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Educational evaluation should prioritise whether students grasp scientific method and reasoning rather than recall of factual detail. Concentrating on a small range of phenomena is often superior pedagogically for teaching method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of specialization to learn method
rubrics_metrics.description: The patient and persistent study of some one branch of natural science ... would be not only sufficient to give a thorough insight into scientific method, but would also enable the student to become a careful observer and possibly an original investigator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages focused, sustained study (specialization) as a route to acquiring scientific method and observational skills; this contrasts with superficial breadth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of scientific method beyond physical science
rubrics_metrics.description: The scientific method of examining facts is not peculiar to one class of phenomena and to one class of workers; it is applicable to social as well as to physical problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the same standards of classification, evidence, and impartial inference when evaluating social or biological claims as when evaluating physical claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear language and avoidance of metaphysical obfuscation
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the language in which scientific results are stated that needs reconsideration... science, as long as it had to carry on a difficult warfare with metaphysics and dogma, ... conceived it best to hide its own deficient organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientific writing and instruction should avoid ambiguous or metaphysical terminology that conceals weak organisation or thought; clarity of language is a criterion of good science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canons of legitimate inference
rubrics_metrics.description: The chapter headings and text list 'The Canons of Legitimate Inference' and topics such as the scientific validity of a conception and of an inference, sense-impressions and consciousness, limits to other-consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inferential standards include: grounding concepts in sensations/observations, assessing validity of conceptions and inferences, recognising limits to what can be inferred about other minds (other-consciousness), and applying precise rules for when an inference is legitimate. (The book develops detailed rules under this rubric.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensations as the ultimate source of materials of knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensations as the ultimate source of the materials of knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientific claims should be traceable to sensory data (observations/measurements); evaluation asks whether the presented concepts and inferences are legitimately connected to observable impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity of external-world inferences and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Attitude of science towards ejects; the external universe; outside and inside myself; the limits to other-consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating claims about an external world or other minds, establish whether the inference from perception to external-reality (or other-consciousness) is warranted and where limits to such inference lie.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning and formulation of scientific law
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the word law and its meanings; natural law relative to man; the two senses of the words 'natural law'; confusion between senses; universality of scientific law; progress in formulating natural law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To evaluate a purported scientific 'law', determine which sense of 'law' is used (relative to human classification or presumed universal regularity), whether the law is formulated clearly, its empirical basis, and whether apparent universality is justified by the scope of observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Man as maker/constructor of natural law (relative laws)
rubrics_metrics.description: Man as the maker of natural law; natural law relative to man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise that some 'laws' may be human-constructed summaries of observed regularities rather than metaphysical imperatives; evaluate laws for their classificatory usefulness and empirical support rather than assumed metaphysical necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause and effect as routine of experience; first causes excluded
rubrics_metrics.description: First causes have no existence for science; cause and effect as the routine of experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientific evaluation treats causation as regularities in experience (patterns) rather than appeal to metaphysical first causes; tests for causal claims should focus on observed routinised sequences and mechanistic explanation where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability and the basis of probabilistic claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Probability as to breaches in the routine of perceptions; probable and provable; the basis of Laplace's theory in an experience of ignorance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating probabilistic claims, distinguish between what is provable and what is probable given ignorance; assess whether probability assignments reflect empirical frequencies, justified priors, or are mere expressions of ignorance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity belongs to conceptions, not perceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Necessity belongs to the world of conceptions, not to that of perceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful not to impute metaphysical necessity to empirical regularities; necessary relations are conceptual tools, and evaluation should separate conceptual necessity from empirical observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Space and time as modes of perception; conceptual vs perceptual distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Space as a mode of perception; time as a mode of perception; conceptual space and conceptual time and their measurement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate claims about space/time by clarifying whether they are about perceptual modes or abstract/conceptual constructs; ensure definitions and measurements are stated consistently and unambiguously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptual rigour in describing motion (geometry of motion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Motion as the mixed mode of perception; conceptual analysis of point-motion, position, map of the path, time-chart, velocity as slope, acceleration as spurt and shunt, curvature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientific descriptions of motion should use precise conceptual tools (charts, diagrams, definitions of velocity and acceleration) and examine relative character of position and motion; clarity and internal consistency are evaluation criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful definition and critique of 'matter' concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: How physicists define matter; does matter occupy space; common-sense view of matter (impenetrable and hard); hardness not characteristic of matter; matter as non-matter in motion; ether hypotheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate propositions about 'matter' by testing definitions, avoiding reliance on common-sense but imprecise attributes (hardness, impenetrability), and examine whether hypotheses (e.g., ether, vortex atoms) have empirical explanatory power and do not reintroduce metaphysics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits to mechanism and critique of Newtonian laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The limits to mechanism; criticism of the Newtonian laws of motion; how far does mechanism extend?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether mechanistic explanations are appropriate for the phenomenon in question (especially in biology), and scrutinise supposed universal mechanical laws for empirical adequacy and conceptual consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of life and criteria for biological explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: The definition of living and lifeless; life defined by secondary characteristics; do the laws of motion apply to life?; origin of life (biogenesis vs abiogenesis); natural selection in inorganic world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating biological claims, require clear operational definitions of 'life', test whether mechanical physics laws apply at relevant levels, and demand empirical grounding for origin-of-life hypotheses; consider secondary characteristics and evolutionary explanations carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of natural selection as explanatory principle beyond biology
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural selection in the inorganic world; natural selection and the history of man; natural selection as a principle in primitive history and social evolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the explanatory scope of natural selection cautiously: evaluate whether variation-and-selection models are empirically supported in the domain claimed and whether alternative mechanisms are excluded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical/social implications should be judged by scientific classification of facts
rubrics_metrics.description: For citizenship, judgments must be based on a clear knowledge of facts, an appreciation of their sequence and relative significance; the scientific frame of mind is essential to good citizenship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy or moral recommendations should be evaluated on the basis of classified factual evidence and careful reasoning rather than partisan interest; the criterion of good scientific reasoning applies to social decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of the sciences: criteria for taxonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Precise and synoptic sciences; abstract and concrete sciences; Spencer's and Comte's classifications; applied mathematics and bio-physics as cross links.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When classifying a discipline, evaluate whether it is synoptic or precise, abstract or concrete, and identify cross-linking fields; taxonomy should reflect the nature of phenomena and methods used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation and pedagogy: use examples, summaries, and literature
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapters include 'Summary and Literature' sections, and the author emphasises arranging material to impart method by focused study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Educational and expository work should include summaries, pointers to literature, and worked examples to teach method; evaluators should look for these pedagogical features as markers of effective scientific communication.
